t: A ball is at the bottom of the hill, moving fast. It has no height. What does it have?
A ball rolls fast along the ground. It is not high up. What does it have?
A ball at ground level moves at speed v. What energy does it possess?
A body at h=0 with velocity v has what form of energy?
sub: It is not high, so it has no height energy. But it is moving — and moving is a kind of energy too.
Height is not the only energy. Moving is energy. The faster you go, the more you have.
Kinetic energy: the energy of motion. A moving ball has it even at ground level.
Kinetic energy KE = ½mv². The energy of motion, present whenever v ≠ 0.

question: A ball moves twice as fast. Does it have twice the moving energy?
Double the speed of a ball. Does its moving energy double?
If v → 2v, what happens to the kinetic energy?
If velocity doubles (at constant m), how does KE change?
options: No, it has FOUR times as much — speed is squared
Yes, twice the speed means twice the energy
No, the energy stays the same
stages.outcome: No, it has FOUR times as much — speed is squared
note: This one surprises almost everyone. Guess what you think.
Predict before checking. The answer is not what intuition says.
Form a hypothesis from KE = ½mv². The v is squared.
Predict. KE ∝ v², so doubling v quadruples KE. Verify in the sim.

t: Launch the ball from a height. Watch the KE bar (blue) grow as it falls — the faster it goes, the more KE.
Launch from height 4. Watch the blue KE bar grow as the ball descends. The faster it moves, the larger the bar.
goal: Launch and watch the KE bar. The faster the ball, the bigger the blue bar.
Launch. Observe KE ∝ v²: the blue bar grows quadratically with speed.

t: Launch from height 2, then height 4. The second ball goes faster — but by how much? Work it out before you check.
Launch from h=2, then h=4. Predict the ratio of speeds at the bottom (use mgh = ½mv²) before testing. Verify the √ relationship.
goal: Launch from different heights. Higher start means more speed — but not linearly more.
Verify: v = √(2gh). Doubling h gives √2 times the speed, not double. KE is quadratic in v.

t: The energy of moving is called kinetic energy. The faster you go, the more you have.
The energy of motion is called kinetic energy. Faster means more — and not just a little more.
Kinetic energy (KE) is the energy of motion: KE = ½mv². The v is squared, so double the speed means four times the energy.
Kinetic energy: KE = ½mv². A scalar quantity, quadratic in velocity. The factor of ½ comes from the work-energy theorem integration.
sub: Double the speed and you get FOUR times the kinetic energy. That is why speed limits matter so much.
KE = ½ × mass × speed × speed. The speed is squared — so 2× speed = 4× energy. This is why braking distance grows fast.
KE = ½mv². The quadratic dependence on v is why a crash at 60 mph has four times the energy of a crash at 30 mph.
The v² dependence is why braking distance scales as v²: d = v²/(2a). Road fatality rates correlate with speed limits precisely because of this.

t: A car at 60 mph has four times the moving energy of a car at 30 mph. That is why speed limits save lives.
A car at 60 mph has four times the kinetic energy of one at 30 mph. Braking distance quadruples. That is why speed limits matter.
KE = ½mv². Double the speed, four times the energy, four times the braking distance. This single equation explains most road safety policy.
The v² dependence makes kinetic energy the dominant factor in crash severity. A 10% speed increase yields a 21% increase in crash energy — the physics behind Vision Zero policy.

options: The energy of being high up
why: Kinetic energy is the energy of motion. A moving ball has it; a still ball does not. The faster you go, the more you have.
Kinetic energy is the energy of motion: KE = ½mv². Any moving object has it, proportional to mass and to speed squared.
KE = ½mv². The energy a body possesses by virtue of its motion. A scalar, always non-negative.
KE = ½mv². The work required to accelerate a body from rest to v. A state function of velocity, not position.

q: A ball moves at 2 m/s. Another ball (same mass) moves at 4 m/s. How much more KE does the faster one have?
Ball A moves at 2 m/s. Ball B (same mass) at 4 m/s. How much more KE does B have?
Two identical masses: v_A = 2 m/s, v_B = 4 m/s. What is KE_B / KE_A?
For equal masses with v_B = 2·v_A, what is the ratio KE_B / KE_A?
options: Four times as much — speed is squared
why: KE = ½ × mass × speed × speed. The speed is squared, so twice the speed means four times the energy. 4 m/s has four times the KE of 2 m/s.
KE = ½mv². B has speed 4 (squared = 16); A has speed 2 (squared = 4). 16/4 = 4. Four times the kinetic energy.
KE ∝ v². (v_B/v_A)² = (4/2)² = 4. B has four times the KE of A.
KE_B/KE_A = (v_B/v_A)² = 4. The quadratic dependence on v is the whole story.
